title: The cost of crossing the spread
objectives: Compute the round-trip cost of crossing the spread.
Turn a spread into an annual cost for a trading strategy.

screens.prose: This is the book for one share. You buy 100 shares at once, change your mind, and sell them straight back. Nobody else trades in between.
screens.question: Tap the price you buy at and the price you sell at.

hints.text: A buy at once needs a seller who is waiting. A sell at once needs a waiting buyer.
Sellers sit above the spread row, buyers below it. Take the best of each.

feedback.correct: You buy at the best ask, £100.14, and sell at the best bid, £100.10.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The buy takes the cheapest seller and the sell takes the highest buyer.

byKey.ask0: You found the sell but not the buy. A buy at once pays the cheapest seller, the best ask.
byKey.bid0: You found the buy but not the sell. A sell at once gets the highest buyer, the best bid.
byKey.ask1: £100.15 is a dearer seller. Your 100 shares fill at £100.14, where 800 are waiting.
byKey.ask2: £100.16 is the dearest seller shown. Your 100 shares fill at £100.14 first.
byKey.bid1: £100.09 is a lower buyer. Your sale fills at £100.10, where 600 are waiting.
byKey.bid2: £100.08 is the lowest buyer shown. Your sale fills at £100.10 first.

explain.text: Both orders take what is waiting at the touch: the buy lifts the ask and the sell hits the bid. The two prices are the two edges of the spread.

screens.prose: You paid £100.14 a share and got back £100.10 a share. The price of the share did not move at all.
screens.question: How much did the round trip of 100 shares cost you, in £?

hints.text: Each share was bought at one price and sold at another.
The loss per share is the gap between the two bold prices.

feedback.correct: £4.00: the whole spread, 4p, on each of 100 shares.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the loss on one share, then multiply by 100.

byKey.half: You charged half the spread. The buy paid 2p over the middle and the sell lost another 2p: 4p in all.
byKey.per-share: That is the loss on one share. You traded 100 of them.
byKey.zero: You used the fact that the price did not move. You still bought high and sold low, 4p apart.
byKey.pence: That is the loss in pence. Divide by 100 to give pounds.

explain.text: You lost the spread, 4p, on every share: $100 \times \text{£}0.04 = \text{£}4.00$. Nothing moved, yet trading at once and back again cost money.

screens.prose: Measure each trade from the mid, £100.12. The buy paid 2p above it and the sell got 2p below it. Each side costs **half the spread**, the **half-spread**.
screens.question: What does one side cost, in basis points of the mid? Give one decimal place.

widget.label: Cost of one side in basis points

hints.text: A basis point is one ten-thousandth of the price.
Divide the 2p by the mid, £100.12.

feedback.correct: 2.0 bp a side; the round trip is twice that, 4.0 bp.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide half the spread by the mid, then multiply by 10,000.

byKey.full: That is the whole spread, the cost of the round trip. One side pays half of it.
byKey.percent: That is the cost in per cent. One basis point is 0.01%, so multiply by 100.

explain.text: Against the mid, the buy paid $\text{£}0.02 / \text{£}100.12 = 2.0$ bp and the sell paid the same. The two halves make the round trip, 4.0 bp, the spread in basis points.

canvas.caption: 2.0 bp a side, 4.0 bp a round trip

screens.prose: A pension fund buys £50,000 of this share and sells it a month later. Suppose the price ends where it started, and the spread is still 4p.

state.caption: Spread 4p on a mid of £100.12: 4.0 bp

screens.question: What do the two trades cost in spreads, in £?

hints.text: Turn the spread into a fraction of the price first.
The round trip costs 4.0 bp, or 0.0004 of the amount traded.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply £50,000 by the round-trip cost as a fraction, 0.04 / 100.12.

byKey.once: You charged one side. The fund bought and then sold, so it paid both halves.
byKey.percent: You read 4p as 4%. The spread is 4p on £100.12, which is 0.04%.
byKey.per-share: That is the cost on one share. The fund bought about 499 shares.

explain.text: The fund bought $50{,}000 / 100.12 \approx 499$ shares and lost 4p on each: about £19.98. In basis points it is quicker: $50{,}000 \times 0.0004 = \text{£}20$.

screens.prose: Share D is quoted £50.00 bid and £50.01 ask. Prices move in 1p ticks, so no spread can be narrower than this one. The mid is £50.005.
screens.question: A dark pool matches your buy at the mid, £50.005. What spread cost does that buy pay?

options.why: You charged half the spread. That is the cost of buying at the ask; this buy paid the mid itself.
You charged the whole spread. Even a buy at the ask pays only half of it against the mid.

options.text: A tick is the least any trade can cost
options.why: The tick is the narrowest gap between quotes. A fill exactly at the mid sits between them and pays nothing against the mid.

hints.text: We measure every cost from the mid.
Where is the fill price compared with the mid?
The fill is at £50.005 and the mid is £50.005.

feedback.correct: A fill at the mid costs nothing against the mid.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the fill price with the mid.

explain.text: A mid fill costs 0 bp, but the cheapest buy on screen is the ask, 1.0 bp above the mid. No quote can sit closer than a tick. Mid-point venues are one way under that floor; level 3 shows their catch.

screens.prose: Three shares, and £10,000 to trade in and out of each. In pence, A and B have the same spread and C looks five times dearer.
screens.question: Fill in each spread in basis points and the round-trip cost on £10,000.

hints.text: Find each mid first, then divide the spread by it.
B's mid is £10.00 and C's is £250.00.
B: $0.04/10 \times 10{,}000 = 40$ bp. C: $0.20/250 \times 10{,}000 = 8$ bp. A round trip costs £1 on £10,000 for each basis point.

feedback.correct: A 4.0 bp, B 40 bp, C 8 bp: B is the dearest by far.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Spread in bp is $10{,}000 \times s/m$, and the round trip on £10,000 is £1 per basis point.

explain.text: Divide each spread by its mid: A 4.0 bp, B 40 bp, C 8 bp. Each basis point of £10,000 is £1, so the round trips cost £4, £40 and £8. In pence B looked as cheap as A; it is ten times dearer.

screens.prose: Back to our £100.12 share. You bought 100 shares at £100.14, the ask on screen when you sent the order. Your broker's report says the fill cost nothing: you got exactly the quoted price.
screens.question: Against the mid, what did that buy cost you per share?

options.why: You measured from the ask. The ask already includes half the spread above the mid, so a buy at the ask is not free.
You charged the whole spread to one trade. The buy pays half; the sell, when it comes, pays the other half.
You measured from the bid. The bid is where you could sell, not the fair middle; measure from the mid.

hints.text: Whose price is the ask? Is it the middle of the market?
The mid is £100.12. How far above it is £100.14?

feedback.correct: 2p a share, 2.0 bp. The report hid the half-spread.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Measure the fill from the mid, £100.12.

byKey.zero: You took the quoted price as the benchmark. A buyer's quote is the ask, and it sits half a spread above the mid.
byKey.full: You charged the round trip to the buy. One side costs half the spread.
byKey.bid: You measured from the bid. The fair middle is the mid.

explain.text: The ask is not the price; it is the price plus half the spread. Measured from the mid, your buy paid 2p a share, £2.00 in all. A report that benchmarks against the quote you crossed always shows zero.

screens.prose: Each £ you trade crosses half the spread. Now scale up to a whole portfolio worth $V$ that turns over $T$ times a year. The spread is $s$ and the mid $m$ throughout.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: Turning over $T$ times means selling $TV$ of old holdings a year
and buying $TV$ of new ones, so $2TV$ is traded in all
Each £ traded pays half the spread: $\dfrac{s}{2m}$

hints.text: Start with how much is traded in a year.
Every turnover has a sell and a buy.
Count the £ traded, $2TV$, then charge each £ the half-spread.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the £ traded first, then charge each £ the half-spread.

byKey.side: The cost per £ only helps once you know how many £ are traded. Count the sells and buys first.
byKey.total: The total multiplies the £ traded by the cost per £, so it comes last.

explain.text: A turnover is a sell plus a buy, so each one costs a full round trip, $s/m$. A fund turning over 300% a year at 10 bp per trade loses $3 \times 2 \times 10 = 60$ bp, or 0.6% a year.

screens.prose: A short-term signal predicts the next move. Its backtest, using mid prices, shows an edge of 3 bp per round trip. Live, it enters and exits with market orders in this share.

state.caption: Spread 1p on a mid of £25.005: 4.0 bp

screens.question: What does it make per round trip after the spread, in bp?

widget.label: Net edge per round trip in basis points

hints.text: A backtest on mid prices trades for free. Live trading does not.
A round trip with market orders pays the whole spread.

feedback.correct: −1 bp: the spread eats the whole edge and more.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the round-trip spread cost, 4 bp, from the 3 bp edge.

byKey.ignored: That is the backtest's edge. Live, every round trip pays the spread.
byKey.half: You charged one side. Entering and exiting are two trades, so the round trip pays the whole 4 bp.
byKey.double: You charged the whole spread on each side. Each side pays half, 2 bp.
byKey.added: You added the spread. Market orders pay it; resting orders that get filled are the ones that earn it.

explain.text: Each round trip pays 4 bp and earns 3 bp, so the strategy loses 1 bp every time it trades. Resting orders on both sides would earn the spread instead, which is why passive fills matter. Level 3 shows they bring risks of their own.

screens.prose: A £1m portfolio is rebalanced every trading day. Each day it sells £25,000 of some holdings and buys £25,000 of others. Its shares have spreads of 10 bp.
screens.question: What do the spreads cost over a year of 252 trading days, in £?

hints.text: How much is traded each day, and what does each £ pay?
Each £ traded pays half the spread, 5 bp.
$50{,}000 \times 0.0005 = \text{£}25$ a day, for 252 days.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Charge 5 bp on the £50,000 traded each day, then multiply by 252.

byKey.once: You charged only the sells, or only the buys. Both sides pay half the spread.
byKey.full: You charged the whole 10 bp spread on each trade. Each single trade pays half of it.
byKey.day: That is one day's cost. Multiply by 252 trading days.

explain.text: £50,000 a day at 5 bp is £25 a day, and 252 days make £6,300. That is 0.63% of the portfolio every year, before fees or impact. A strategy has to beat that just to break even.

ideas: A buy at once pays the ask and a sell gets the bid, so a round trip loses the whole spread.
Measured from the mid, each side costs half the spread: $\frac{s}{2m}$, or 2.0 bp a side on a 4p spread at £100.12.
Costs scale with trading: a portfolio turning over $T$ times a year pays $T\,s/m$ of its value.

formula.name: Cost of crossing
formula.note: Measure from the mid $m$, never from the quote you crossed.

summary.trap: A fill at the ask is not free: the ask already sits half a spread above the mid.

quiz.prose: A fund turns over its portfolio 300% a year. It pays 10 bp each time it buys or sells.
quiz.question: What do spreads cost it a year?

options.why: You counted one trade per turnover. Replacing a holding means a sell and a buy.
You charged one trade a year. Turning over 300% means three sells and three buys.
You read 10 bp as 0.1% but then slipped a place. Six trades at 10 bp is 60 bp, 0.6%.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the sells and buys in a year, then charge each 10 bp.

explain.text: Three turnovers are three sells and three buys: six trades at 10 bp each, 60 bp. That is 0.6% of the fund lost every year to spreads.

quiz.prose: A small company's share is quoted £4.98 bid and £5.02 ask. You buy £20,000 of it and later sell at the same quotes.
quiz.question: What did the round trip cost in spreads, in £?

widget.label: Round-trip cost in pounds
widget.accept: £160: the spread is 4p on £5.00, 80 bp, and $20{,}000 \times 0.008 = 160$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the spread in bp of the £5.00 mid, then apply it to £20,000.

byKey.once: You charged one side. A round trip pays the whole spread.
byKey.pence: You multiplied the 4p spread by 20,000 shares. £20,000 buys only 4,000 shares.

explain.text: The spread is $0.04 / 5.00 = 0.008$, or 80 bp. A round trip of £20,000 costs $20{,}000 \times 0.008 = \text{£}160$: 4,000 shares at 4p.

quiz.prose: A share is quoted £199.90 bid and £200.10 ask.
quiz.question: What does a single market buy cost against the mid, in bp?

widget.label: Cost of one side in basis points

feedback.generic: Not quite right. One side pays half the spread; divide by the mid.

byKey.full: That is the round trip. A single buy pays half the spread.
byKey.pence: That is the spread in pence. Halve it and divide by the mid.

explain.text: The spread is 20p on a £200.00 mid, 10 bp. A single buy pays half of it, 5 bp.

quiz.prose: A share is quoted one tick wide: £20.00 bid and £20.01 ask. You must buy at once on this exchange's book.
quiz.question: Which statement is right?

options.text: You pay half a tick over the mid, 2.5 bp, and no quote on this book can make it less
A one-tick spread is free to cross
options.why: You treated the narrowest spread as no spread. Half a tick is still paid on every buy.

options.text: You pay 5 bp over the mid
options.why: 5 bp is the whole spread. One side pays half of it against the mid.

options.text: The spread will soon narrow to half a tick
options.why: Quotes sit on the tick grid. Nothing between £20.00 and £20.01 can be quoted here.

feedback.correct: One tick is the floor: half a tick per side.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the half-spread in bp of the £20.005 mid.

explain.text: The spread is 1p on £20.005, 5.0 bp, so a buy at the ask pays 2.5 bp over the mid. Quotes live on the tick grid, so a one-tick spread is as tight as this book gets.
